Webb observes mostly in infrared rather than visible light, which lets it see through dust clouds and detect galaxies whose light has stretched red over billions of years of travel. That combination lets it pick out objects up to a hundred times fainter than Hubble can manage, reaching back to within roughly 180 million years of the Big Bang.

Japan's earlier Lambda 4S rockets had failed repeatedly to reach orbit, built by the University of Tokyo's Institute of Space and Aeronautical Science rather than a state space agency. On 11 February 1970 the fifth attempt succeeded, carrying the small satellite Ohsumi into orbit.

The launch put Japan fourth in the world to orbit a satellite on a home-built booster, after the Soviet Union, the United States and France, and ahead of China by two months. Ohsumi itself carried little instrumentation; the achievement was getting a homemade rocket into space at all.

On 14 May 1796, Edward Jenner scraped material from a cowpox blister on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes and worked it into two small cuts on the arm of eight year old James Phipps, the son of his gardener. Phipps ran a mild fever but recovered within days, matching a belief already common among Gloucestershire dairy workers that catching cowpox warded off smallpox.

The real test came on 1 July, when Jenner deliberately exposed Phipps to smallpox matter and the boy showed no sign of infection. Jenner had not discovered the cowpox connection himself; his contribution was proving, through repeated challenge, that the immunity transferred and could be passed on from person to person, which turned folk observation into a repeatable medical procedure.

Frank Whittle was a young RAF officer when he patented a turbojet design in January 1930, years before anyone would build one. The Air Ministry showed so little interest that it refused to pay the five pound renewal fee, and Whittle, unable to cover it himself while studying at Cambridge, let the patent lapse in 1935.

He pressed on anyway, forming Power Jets Ltd with private backers. The Gloster E.28/39, powered by his engine, finally flew from Cranwell on 15 May 1941, seventeen minutes that proved the concept, though a German jet had already flown in secret nine months earlier.

Monks at Heungdeok temple, near modern Cheongju, printed Jikji in 1377 using individually cast metal type, a Zen teacher's compilation of sayings and biographies handed down from earlier Buddhist masters. It was not Korea's first use of the technique: government records describe a book cast in metal type as early as 1234, well over a century before Gutenberg, though no copy of that earlier work has survived.

Only the second of Jikji's two volumes still exists, its final pages missing. A French diplomat in Seoul collected it in the 1890s, it passed through a Paris auction in 1911 to the collector Henri Vever, and his family gave it to the National Library of France in 1950. UNESCO recognised it in 2001 as the oldest surviving book printed anywhere with movable metal type.

King Seonjo ordered the project in 1596, after Japanese invasions had scattered Korea's medical texts and left ordinary people without reliable treatments. The royal physician Heo Jun led the compilation, finishing it in 1610 under Seonjo's successor, Gwanghaegun, who had the finished work printed in 1613 as the Dongeuibogam.

Rather than organising illness by disease name, Heo Jun grouped remedies by the bodily organ affected, drawing together two thousand years of Korean and Chinese medical writing into one reference. The approach spread across East Asia and the text is still consulted by practitioners of traditional medicine; UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World Register in 2009.

King Sejong's court did not build one laboratory but staffed a whole workshop of instrument makers, the best known of them Jang Yeong-sil, a former government slave promoted for his skill in metalwork. Between roughly 1433 and 1442 they turned out a self-striking water clock, a bronze sundial with seasonal markings, and an armillary sphere driven by a waterwheel to track the stars automatically.

The standardised rain gauge, the cheugugi, followed in 1441, reportedly built to a design proposed by the crown prince rather than by Jang himself. Sejong ordered a matching gauge sent to every provincial office so rainfall could be compared across the kingdom for the first time, turning a court curiosity into a nationwide agricultural record.

Jang Yeong-sil, an engineer of low birth whom King Sejong had promoted for his skill, travelled to China to study existing water clock designs after earlier attempts failed. He returned in 1434 and built the Jagyeongnu, a clock that struck the hour on its own using a bell, a gong and a drum rather than needing a human timekeeper to watch and announce it.

Water flowing at a steady rate through a chain of vessels released iron balls that tripped levers at fixed intervals, ringing the instruments and turning twelve wooden figures to show the hour visually as well as by sound. No original Jagyeongnu survives, but Joseon records were detailed enough that later reconstructions could reproduce its mechanism for museum display.

Silhak scholars were mostly shut out of government office, which freed them to write what officials could not. They argued that Neo-Confucian philosophy had drifted into abstraction while peasants worked exhausted land with medieval tools, and that land reform and better technique mattered more than ritual correctness.

Yi Ik, born in 1681, founded one strand of the movement pressing for redistribution of farmland; later figures such as Chong Yagyong pushed the same practical bent into engineering and administration. None of them held power to enact their proposals, so Silhak's influence on Joseon farming was mostly through the ideas it left behind rather than any single decree.

James Joule ran his family's Manchester brewery by day and treated physics as a serious hobby. Around 1843 he built an apparatus in which falling weights turned a paddle wheel inside an insulated barrel of water, converting a measured amount of mechanical work directly into a measured rise in temperature.

The result was a fixed exchange rate between work and heat, roughly 4.19 joules per calorie, showing the two were the same quantity in different forms rather than separate phenomena. It took years for the wider scientific community, sceptical of a brewer's home experiments, to accept a number now named after him.

Louis Glass and William Arnold did not build a new machine, they modified one. Their coin-operated music player was an ordinary Edison Class M phonograph fitted with a mechanism that only released the crank once a nickel dropped in. It debuted at the Palais Royale Saloon in San Francisco in 1889.

There was no speaker. Patrons listened through one of four rubber tubes plugged into their ears, so several people could pay to hear the same cylinder at once without the rest of the saloon overhearing for free. That coin mechanism, patented as a Coin Actuated Attachment for Phonograph, is what turned recorded sound from a demonstration novelty into paying entertainment.

Austrian engineer Viktor Kaplan patented an adjustable-blade water turbine in 1912 and refined the design over the following years. Earlier Francis turbines worked well where a river dropped a great height, but lost efficiency badly wherever the head of water was low, which ruled out many otherwise promising sites for hydropower.

Kaplan's turbine solved that by combining propeller-like blades that pitch automatically with adjustable wicket gates, so the machine keeps its efficiency across a wide range of water flow and level. Commercial adoption only began in the 1920s, but the design became the standard choice for low-head hydroelectric stations on rivers worldwide.

Kepler had spent years wrestling with Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars, whose orbit refused to fit a circle no matter how the numbers were arranged. In Astronomia Nova, published in 1609, he gave up the circle entirely and described the planet's path as an ellipse with the sun sitting at one focus, not the centre.

The same book carried a second finding: a line drawn from a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest near the sun and slowest far from it. Kepler reached both results by working through Mars alone, then generalised them to every known planet.

Madhava of Sangamagrama, working near modern Tirur in Kerala, found infinite series for sine, cosine and the arctangent, and used them to compute pi to nine decimal places as 3.141592653. His pupils carried the work forward for two centuries, producing what historians treat as the first known power series outside the simple geometric case.

Whether any of this reached Isaac Newton or Gottfried Leibniz remains unproven; no manuscript trail connects Kerala's results to Europe, and the two men are credited with independently welding similar ideas into a single system built on the derivative and the integral. Madhava's school never made that unification, which is why the achievement is usually described as anticipating calculus rather than inventing it.

Stephanie Kwolek was not trying to stop bullets. In 1965, working at DuPont on lighter tyres for a feared petrol shortage, she produced a polymer solution that came out cloudy and thin, the kind of batch a chemist would normally discard.

She asked a technician, Charles Smullen, to spin it into fibre anyway. It refused to break the way nylon did, and testing showed a fibre roughly five times stronger than steel of the same weight. DuPont brought the refined version to market as Kevlar in 1971, and it went into vests rather than tyres.

For roughly the first twenty-five years of his life, al-Biruni worked in Khwarezm, the region around the lower Amu Darya, studying jurisprudence, grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy under scholars at the Khwarezmshah court. This broad early training, rather than any single teacher, is what let him later move fluently between subjects that Islamic scholarship usually kept separate.

Political upheaval in Khwarezm eventually pushed him toward the court of the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud, whose campaigns into India from 1017 gave al-Biruni years of direct access to Indian scholars, texts and observatories. The resulting study of Indian science and religion, finished around 1030, grew directly out of the grounding he had built in Khwarezm rather than replacing it.

In Gurganj, capital of Khwarezm, the Ma'mun Academy gathered scholars under the polymath al-Biruni, who wrote over a hundred works spanning astronomy, mathematics, geography and chemistry. Ibn Sina, then a young physician, worked alongside him, along with Abu Sahl al-Masihi and Abu'l-Khayr al-Khammar.

The academy carried forward a tradition of translation and inquiry begun two centuries earlier in Baghdad's House of Wisdom. Al-Biruni used it to measure the earth's circumference and to calculate the longitude between Baghdad and Khwarezm by timing a lunar eclipse observed from both cities at once, work he later folded into treatises on geodesy and astronomy.

Working at Baghdad's House of Wisdom under Caliph al-Ma'mun, al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise on solving linear and quadratic equations by systematic restoration and balancing, calling the method al-jabr, the Arabic word that became algebra. Rather than presenting isolated tricks, he set out general procedures that could be applied to any equation of the same shape.

A separate book on calculation with Hindu numerals, now lost in Arabic but preserved through a twelfth-century Latin translation, carried the place-value digits and the zero into Europe. That Latin version's title, rendering his name as Algoritmi, is the direct source of the modern word algorithm.

Willem Kolff built his first dialysis machine in Nazi-occupied Netherlands using orange juice cans, salvaged auto parts and sausage casings as the filtering membrane, since proper equipment was unobtainable. Blood was drawn through the casings, wound around a rotating drum, so waste products could pass out into a surrounding bath while the blood itself stayed inside.

Over the next two years all fifteen patients he treated with the device died, mostly too far into kidney failure to be saved. In 1945 a 67-year-old woman in a uraemic coma recovered after treatment on his machine, the first success. Kolff later gave away his designs rather than patent them, and dialysis spread from that improvised drum.

An open bonfire cannot hold a steady, high heat, and pottery fired that way stays porous and weak. Building an enclosed chamber that trapped and concentrated the fire's heat let potters reach temperatures a campfire never could, hardening clay all the way through instead of just baking its surface.

The same enclosed-heat principle, once mastered for pottery, carried straight over to firing bricks, and later to smelting ores that needed similarly sustained temperatures. A kiln is, in effect, a controllable furnace, and control over heat rather than a single new material was the real advance it delivered.

Amazon's first Kindle went on sale on 19 November 2007 for 399 dollars, roughly what a modest laptop cost at the time. It had no touchscreen: a physical keyboard and a scroll wheel handled navigation, and a built-in dictionary plus a stripped-down Wikipedia lookup sat alongside the free wireless delivery Amazon called Whispernet. Its e-ink screen showed six shades of grey and no colour at all.

Amazon never confirmed exact early sales, and estimates for how many had shipped by December 2009 ranged from around 1.5 million to over three million depending on the source. The device carried Amazon's own proprietary format, AZW, which locked buyers to its store much as the iPod had done for music, and set the template every rival e-reader would spend years copying.

William Lee built his frame in 1589 to knit stockings mechanically, forming loops with rows of hooked needles instead of a pair of hand-held ones. The often-told tale that Elizabeth I refused him a patent to protect hand-knitters is an account that only appears in the nineteenth century, long after Lee's own lifetime, and historians treat it as invented.

Whatever the reason, Lee found no backing in England and moved to France with his brother and several workmen, where Henry IV supported his workshop at Rouen. After the king's assassination in 1610 the support dried up, and Lee died abroad with the venture unfinished. His workers carried the frame back to Nottingham, which became the centre of English framework knitting.

George Eastman's camera came preloaded with enough film for 100 photographs and cost 25 dollars, cheap enough for an amateur to buy without ever learning to load a plate or mix a chemical bath. His slogan told buyers exactly what that meant: they pressed the button, Kodak did the rest.

Once the roll was finished, the whole camera, not just the film, was mailed back to Eastman's factory in Rochester along with ten dollars. The company developed the pictures, reloaded fresh film, and returned camera and prints together. That single decision, selling a service rather than just a device, is what turned photography into a hobby for people who had never touched a darkroom.

La Salle and his party paddled down the Mississippi by canoe, reaching the Gulf of Mexico in April 1682. There he planted a cross and claimed the entire river basin for France, naming it Louisiane after King Louis XIV, a claim covering land he had barely glimpsed and that stretched across territory already inhabited by dozens of nations.

The claim outran his ability to hold it. A later expedition meant to found a colony near the river's mouth missed it by hundreds of kilometres, landing instead on the Texas coast, and the venture collapsed into mutiny. La Salle was shot dead by his own men near the Trinity River in March 1687, ambushed while walking to meet one of the conspirators.

The patty served on 5 August 2013 in London was built from more than 20,000 thin strips of muscle tissue, cultured over two years by Mark Post's team at Maastricht University from a cow's stem cells. Chef Richard McGeown cooked it in butter and coloured it with beetroot juice and saffron, since the tissue itself had grown pale rather than red.

Food researcher Hanni Rutzler and critic Josh Schonwald ate the first bites on camera; Rutzler called the texture close to meat, though drier, and said she would not have picked it out as fake in a blind test. Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who had funded the project anonymously, wanted proof that meat could be produced without raising or killing an animal.

Sap tapped from lacquer trees hardens on contact with air into a tough, glossy, waterproof film, a property no other natural coating of the period could match. The earliest known lacquerware, a red wooden bowl from the Hemudu culture in China, dates to around this time, and separate finds in Japan's Jomon period suggest the same technique was worked out there too.

Because raw lacquer sap is toxic to handle and slow to cure properly, working it demanded skill passed down over generations rather than a technique anyone could pick up quickly. That difficulty is part of why lacquerware stayed a prized, labour-intensive craft across China, Japan and Korea for thousands of years afterward.

Lagrange claimed his treatise contained no diagrams at all, calling it a purely analytical work built on algebra and calculus. Where Newton's approach tracked forces acting on a body, Lagrange described motion through a single scalar quantity, the difference between kinetic and potential energy, and let calculus of variations grind out the equations of motion.

He wrote most of it years before publication and had to be persuaded to release it; a printer in Paris finally issued it in 1788. The method proved so general that it later underpinned quantum mechanics and field theory, areas Lagrange could not have imagined, because it does not care what coordinates describe the system.

Diophantus had noticed centuries earlier that small numbers could be written as sums of four square numbers, and the French mathematician Claude Gaspard Bachet de Meziriac stated the pattern as a conjecture in 1621 while translating Diophantus into Latin.

It took until 1770 for Joseph-Louis Lagrange to prove the claim held for every positive integer, using a method built on earlier work by Euler. Adrien-Marie Legendre extended the result decades later, and the theorem still carries Lagrange's name despite the century and a half separating conjecture from proof.

Laika did not survive her flight for days as Soviet reports first claimed. Telemetry from Sputnik 2, launched on 3 November 1957, showed her dying within about five to seven hours, when the capsule's insulation failed to separate properly from the booster and cabin temperatures climbed past 40 degrees Celsius. There was never a plan to bring her home; the craft had no re-entry system.

The true cause stayed hidden for decades. Only in October 2002 did Dimitri Malashenkov, one of the mission's scientists, admit publicly that Laika had overheated by the fourth orbit, and that building a reliable temperature control system in the time available had proved impossible. The Soviet press had instead let the world believe she lived on painlessly for a week before a planned euthanasia.

In 1903, French chemist Édouard Bénédictus dropped a glass flask in his laboratory and found it had cracked without shattering into fragments. The flask had held a solution of cellulose nitrate that had evaporated, leaving a thin plastic film coating the inside of the glass, which held the broken pieces together.

Bénédictus set the discovery aside until he read a newspaper account of two women badly cut by broken windscreen glass in a car crash. He patented his laminated glass in 1909 and founded the Société du Verre Triplex in 1911 to sell it for automobile windscreens, the use that eventually made the material standard worldwide.

Thirteenth and fourteenth century European infantry lengthened their spears into pikes several metres long, so several ranks of men could present a wall of points that deterred a mounted charge a shorter weapon could not stop at range. Cavalry lances lengthened too, tapered and braced under the arm with a lance rest, a device that appeared by the late fourteenth century, to survive the shock of a couched charge at full gallop.

Neither change came from one battle: they were incremental responses as infantry and knights each adjusted to the other's equipment over generations. Flemish spearmen broke mounted knights at Courtrai in 1302 and Scottish schiltrons did likewise at Bannockburn in 1314, decades before Swiss pike squares made heavily armoured cavalry far less decisive on open ground.

A Song brigadier remembered as Lou Qianxia buried a cast-iron bomb, called an enormous bomb, in the path of Mongol troops invading Guangxi in 1277, timed to explode when the enemy disturbed it rather than when a soldier lit a fuse by hand. Later Chinese accounts describe trigger mechanisms as simple as a cord that toppled a weight, spinning a flint wheel to strike sparks into the powder.

Nothing about the 1277 device survives except the written record of the campaign, so the technical detail comes mostly from a fuller description compiled decades afterward in the military text Huolongjing, written under the early Ming. The core idea, an explosive charge set off by an unsuspecting enemy's own movement rather than a soldier's hand, needed no gunpowder refinement beyond what existing Chinese bombs already used.

Seiko Epson released the HX-20 in Japan in July 1982, sized to fit inside an A4 notebook and weighing about 1.6 kilograms. Its four-line, twenty-character LCD screen and a small built-in dot-matrix printer meant a user could write a program and read the printed result without plugging into anything else.

Rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries kept it running for roughly fifty hours in BASIC, an endurance few later laptops matched. It sold well in Japan but never took off elsewhere, and history remembers the Radio Shack TRS-80 Model 100, released a year later, as the notebook computer that actually made the format commercially successful.

Theodore Maiman built his laser at Hughes Research Laboratories in Malibu on 16 May 1960, using a small rod of synthetic ruby wrapped in a coiled flash lamp rather than the gas systems most physicists assumed would come first. Pumped with a burst of light, the ruby emitted a narrow beam in which every wave matched every other, the property Maiman called coherent light.

Physical Review Letters rejected his paper twice before Nature published it in August 1960, a decision the maser pioneer Charles Townes later called one of the most important short articles the journal ever printed. Maiman and Hughes announced the device to the press on 7 July 1960 in Manhattan, and working lasers of other kinds followed within months once Maiman had shown one could exist at all.

Ancient Egyptian woodworkers turned bowls and furniture legs on a two-person lathe: one worker pulled a rope wound around the workpiece back and forth while a second held a cutting tool against the spinning wood. Egyptian tomb paintings from around the thirteenth century BCE show this exact arrangement, among the earliest depictions of the technique anywhere.

The bow lathe, which let a single worker spin the workpiece with a bow while cutting, developed later and spread through the ancient Near East and Mediterranean. Both versions produced round, symmetrical objects, cups, spindles, chair legs, faster and more consistently than carving by hand, and the underlying idea, rotate the material rather than the tool, still underlies every powered lathe in use now.

Antoine Lavoisier did not rename chemistry's substances alone. In 1787 he submitted a new naming system to the French Academy of Sciences together with Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau, Claude-Louis Berthollet and Antoine Francois de Fourcroy, replacing names such as oil of vitriol and flowers of zinc with compound names built from a substance's elements.

The new system, published as Methode de nomenclature chimique, assumed Lavoisier's own theory that combustion involved oxygen rather than the release of phlogiston, so adopting the names meant implicitly adopting his chemistry too. Many of its logical compound names, such as sulphuric acid and carbon dioxide, are still in use.

Lavoisier began by heating phosphorus and sulfur in sealed vessels and weighing them before and after, finding they gained mass rather than losing it, the opposite of what phlogiston theory predicted. He traced that gained weight to a component of air, which he isolated and named oxygen in 1778, from Greek for acid-former.

He then turned to breathing. Memoirs he read to the Academy of Sciences from 1777 argued that an animal consumes the same gas a flame does, and later calorimeter work with Laplace showed a guinea pig produced heat at roughly the rate a burning candle would, given the same volume of oxygen used. Respiration, he concluded, was a slow form of combustion.

Edwin Beard Budding worked at a textile mill and adapted a rotary blade designed for trimming the nap off woollen cloth into a machine that could cut grass to an even height. He patented it on 31 August 1830, insisting on a witness clause in the agreement because he thought the device might look ridiculous enough for people to laugh at him pushing it.

Regent's Park Zoological Gardens and several Oxford colleges bought early machines, and Ransomes began building licensed copies by 1832. The mower made close-cropped turf affordable at scale, and level, evenly cut ground became the standard surface for the football pitches, bowling greens and tennis courts codified later in the century.

Gaston Plante built his lead-acid cell in Paris in 1859 from two lead sheets separated by rubber strips, rolled into a spiral and immersed in dilute sulphuric acid. Unlike earlier batteries, it could be recharged by pushing a current back through it, and it kept working after being drained.

Plante first used his batteries to light train carriages while they stood at stations, a small demonstration of a much larger idea. The same chemistry, lead plates in acid, still starts petrol and diesel engines today, making it one of the longest-serving inventions in continuous use.

John Roebuck began producing sulfuric acid in Birmingham in 1746 by burning sulfur and saltpetre inside chambers lined with lead rather than the small glass vessels chemists had used before. Lead resisted the acid, cost less than glass, and could be built up to room size, so a batch that once yielded ounces could now yield hundreds of kilograms.

The jump in scale mattered because sulfuric acid was becoming the workhorse of an industrialising chemical trade, used in bleaching textiles, refining metals and later making fertiliser. Roebuck's chambers, refined over the following century, remained the standard method of manufacture for close to two hundred years.

Lead ore melts and separates from rock at a lower temperature than copper does, which is likely why people worked it out early even though the metal itself, soft and heavy, was not especially useful for tools. What mattered was the process: heat the right stone hot enough and it gives up pure metal.

That discovery mattered more as a template than as a product. The same basic idea, heating ore past the point where metal separates from slag, was later pushed further to smelt copper and eventually bronze, so lead's real importance is as an early rehearsal for metallurgy rather than for anything made of lead itself.

Nick Holonyak Jr built the first practical visible LED at General Electric's laboratory near Syracuse on 9 October 1962, using a gallium arsenide phosphide alloy in place of the plain gallium arsenide that earlier infrared diodes had relied on. Cooled to low temperatures the device behaved as a laser; at room temperature it simply glowed a steady red, dim by later standards but visible to the eye without special equipment.

Holonyak said soon afterward, in print in early 1963, that diodes like his would eventually replace the incandescent bulb Edison had built decades before. Colleagues at the time treated the prediction as bold; LEDs took another four decades to reach the brightness and efficiency needed to genuinely compete with filament lighting in ordinary homes.

Leeuwenhoek was a Delft cloth merchant with no university training, working from lenses he made himself by heating and pulling glass rods into tiny spheres barely wider than a pinhead. Fitted into a small hand-held frame, one of these could magnify roughly 270 times, far beyond the compound microscopes of his day, and in 1676 he used one to describe what he called animalcules swimming in rainwater and, later, in scrapings from his own teeth.

The Royal Society in London, which he wrote to in Dutch, doubted a tradesman could see what university-trained scholars could not, and asked several independent witnesses to confirm it before accepting his account in 1677. Leeuwenhoek never explained his lens-making method to anyone, so for decades no one else could reliably see what he had already recorded.

Leibniz had sketched binary counting as early as 1679, but his fullest account, Explication de l'Arithmetique Binaire, appeared in 1703. It set out how to write any number using only 0 and 1, and worked through addition and multiplication in the new notation.

He was not the first European to notice the idea; Francis Bacon and John Napier had both toyed with binary-like schemes decades earlier, and Thomas Harriot worked out a binary system without publishing it. What made Leibniz's paper different was its ambition: he tied the pattern of 0s and 1s to the hexagrams of the ancient Chinese Book of Changes, reading it as evidence of a universal mathematical order underlying creation.

Mesopotamian farmers along the Tigris and Euphrates raised earthen banks beside the rivers to hold floodwater away from fields and settlements, part of a wider network of canals that also carried water outward for irrigation. The two systems worked together: levees kept the rivers in their channels, canals let farmers release water on their own terms.

The Indus Valley settlements built around 2600 BCE took a different approach, relying more on wells, reservoirs and drainage than on riverside embankments. Both regions were answering the same problem, a river that fed their fields and could just as easily drown them, with solutions shaped by their own terrain.

Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery west within a year of buying the Louisiana Territory, wanting a river route to the Pacific and a record of what he had just bought. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark left near St Louis in May 1804 with about thirty men, working up the Missouri and over the Continental Divide.

Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman travelling with her infant son and her husband Toussaint Charbonneau, was not the party's guide, but her presence signalled peaceful intent to tribes along the route and her interpreting proved essential. The party reached the Pacific in November 1805 and returned to St Louis in September 1806, having mapped territory no American expedition had crossed before.

A glass jar half filled with water, wrapped in foil and stoppered with a wire running down into the liquid, could hold a shock strong enough to knock a grown man off his feet. Ewald von Kleist built one in 1745; Pieter van Musschenbroek at Leiden found the same effect independently soon after, and it is his university's name that stuck.

Musschenbroek reportedly described the jolt as one he would not take again for the whole kingdom of France. The jar let experimenters store and release charge on demand instead of generating it fresh each time, turning static electricity from a parlour trick into something that could be measured, compared and eventually put to use.

Assyrian palace libraries, including the collection later assembled by Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, kept tablets separated by subject into different rooms: government records in one, astronomy in another, law and history elsewhere. Clay labels or coloured marks identified a tablet's contents, and colophons, notes scribes added at the end of a text, recorded its title, owner or place in a series.

Round tablets typically held agricultural records while four-sided ones recorded financial transactions, a shape-based sorting layered on top of the subject divisions. None of this amounted to a single master index the way a modern library catalogue works, but it let a scribe hunting for a particular omen text or royal inscription go straight to the right room and shelf.

Johann Wolfgang Dobereiner built his lamp in 1823 around a simple reaction: zinc dropped into dilute sulfuric acid produced hydrogen gas, which a valve directed onto a sponge of platinum. The platinum catalysed the hydrogen's combination with air so vigorously that the heat alone ignited the gas, no spark or flint required.

It was the first commercial device to exploit catalysis, and it sold well beyond the chemistry: over a million were made during the 1820s, with a single Thuringian workshop becoming the world's largest producer. Reloading meant replacing cheap zinc and acid, and the design stayed in use as a fire-lighting tool into the 1880s.

Before any tower existed, sailors found harbours by fires lit on hilltops. The Pharos of Alexandria turned that improvisation into architecture, a purpose-built structure marking a port entrance rather than warning ships off a reef, and it stood until earthquakes brought it down between 956 and 1323.

The Tower of Hercules on Spain's Galician coast still stands, giving a rare direct look at how these towers were actually built rather than relying on coins and mosaics from Alexandria, Ostia and Laodicea. Its survival, unlike the Pharos, is what makes ancient lighthouse construction legible today.

Franklin had already worked out that lightning was an electrical discharge and sketched a pointed metal rod to draw it safely to earth in 1749, years before the kite experiment made him famous. The device was simple: an iron spike above the roofline, wired down the outside wall to a rod driven into the ground.

Philadelphia buildings carried the first rods within a few years, and the idea spread through the colonies and Europe faster than almost any of Franklin's other work. He refused to patent it, publishing the design instead so any builder could copy it without paying him a shilling.

Otto Lilienthal's Normal-Segelapparat, built from 1894, was the world's first series-produced aircraft, with at least nine sold to other flying enthusiasts. Made of willow and cotton fabric, its 22-foot wingspan let Lilienthal steer by swinging his own hips and legs to shift his centre of gravity.

Lilienthal made more than two thousand glides across five years, filming and photographing them, and the Wright brothers later called him the most important nineteenth-century pioneer of flight. He died in August 1896, a day after a stall broke his glider's frame and threw him fifty feet to the ground.

Naturalists before Carl Linnaeus described species in sprawling Latin phrases, so a single plant might carry a name running to a dozen words. His Systema Naturae, printed in the Netherlands in 1735, began as a slim twelve pages sorting plants by counting their stamens and pistils.

The system grew enormously over later editions, reaching roughly 4,400 animal species and 7,700 plant species by 1758, and it settled into the two word genus and species naming still used today. Not everyone adopted it at once. The English botanist Philip Miller kept using an older classification for years before switching over.

Sony's research had been chasing a lighter, rechargeable alternative to nickel cadmium cells for its camcorders since the mid 1980s, building on cathode work by John Goodenough and anode research by Akira Yoshino. In 1991 Sony began selling the first commercial lithium ion cell, using a carbon anode instead of pure lithium metal to avoid the fire risk of earlier designs.

The format's energy density let manufacturers shrink camcorders, then laptops, then phones, without shrinking their run time. Goodenough, Yoshino and Stanley Whittingham later shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the underlying chemistry, decades after Sony had already turned it into a shelf product.

Livingstone had not been heard from in years when Stanley, sent by a New York newspaper, tracked him to the lakeside town of Ujiji in 1871. It was Livingstone's own servant who first spotted the approaching party and shouted a warning, not Stanley who made the famous opening remark.

Stanley later wrote that he greeted the older man with the line 'Dr Livingstone, I presume', but the words appear nowhere in his contemporaneous journal. They surface only in a newspaper summary of his letters published the following year, which suggests the line was composed afterward for the story rather than spoken at the lake.

Mesopotamian lenders wrote their terms into clay rather than trusting memory. The Code of Hammurabi, around 1792 to 1750 BC, required a repayment schedule and maturity date fixed in the contract itself, building on a practice of recording interest agreements on tablets that already reached back to around 2000 BC.

Temples, not private bankers, ran much of this system: they held deposits, charged a storage fee of roughly one sixtieth on gold kept with them, and issued seed-grain loans repaid after harvest. That template of written terms and institutional lending outlasted the cities that first used it.

The oldest known lock was not Egyptian. One was recovered from the ruins of Nineveh in ancient Assyria, and locks of this general age run to more than six thousand years old, well before the wooden pin device usually credited to Egypt.

The Egyptian version worked by gravity: wooden pins dropped into holes drilled through a sliding bolt, jamming it in place, and a key lifted the pins clear so the bolt could move. The same principle, a set of pins held by gravity or a spring until a matching key raises them, still runs the modern Yale lock.

Most of the gain came later than the card's date, once Parliament began chartering turnpike trusts that paid for road upkeep out of tolls rather than parish labour. Between 1750 and 1800 the London to Edinburgh journey shrank from about twelve days to four, and Manchester to London fell from three days to twenty-eight hours.

Better roads meant faster coach schedules and fewer carriages broken on ruts, while at sea more reliable rigging and, later, John Harrison's marine chronometers let captains fix a ship's longitude instead of guessing at it. None of this was one invention: it was tolls, surveying and small mechanical fixes accumulating over decades until a journey that once needed a fortnight took days.

What is written down is not the bow's invention but a witness to it. Around 1188 the churchman Gerald of Wales described the bows of Gwent, made of elm rather than yew, as strong enough for close fighting as well as long shots.

Gerald's proof is a single grim anecdote: a Welsh arrow went through a knight's mail-protected thigh, his leather tunic, his saddle, and killed the horse beneath him. It was that account, not a manufacturer's record, that fixed the weapon's reputation before the English army had adopted it.

Gold knucklebones, beads and bracelets from graves at the Varna Necropolis in Bulgaria, dated to roughly 4550 to 4450 BC, are the earliest known objects made this way. A craftsman shaped the object first in wax, packed clay around it, then heated the mould until the wax ran out through a channel, leaving a cavity for molten metal.

The method let a caster reproduce fine detail, texture, undercuts, thin limbs, that hammering or carving metal directly could never achieve, at the cost of destroying the mould with every single casting. That trade-off, one mould per object, is exactly why lost-wax pieces from this period are unique rather than part of a matched set.

Sometime between about 500 and 800 CE, Taino-related people set out from Hispaniola and Cuba in dugout canoes and began settling the Bahamas, one route running from Hispaniola to the Caicos Islands and another from Cuba to Great Inagua. Over the following centuries their descendants, called the Lucayans, spread through the archipelago, reaching a population estimated near 40,000.

Columbus made landfall among them in October 1492 and abducted several Lucayans from the island he renamed San Salvador. Spanish slavers then valued them for their diving skill in the pearl fisheries; Amerigo Vespucci shipped 232 to Spain in 1500, and organised removals to Hispaniola followed after 1509. By 1520, slavers searching the Bahamas could find only eleven Lucayans left alive.

Donald Johanson and his graduate student Tom Gray were about to give up their survey of a gully near Hadar, Ethiopia, on 24 November 1974 when Johanson spotted an arm bone in the dirt. Three weeks of excavation turned up several hundred fragments, roughly 40 percent of a single skeleton, an unusually complete find for a hominin over three million years old.

The name came from camp, not the field. The team played the Beatles' Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds on a tape recorder that night, and Pamela Alderman suggested calling the skeleton Lucy. The species it belonged to, Australopithecus afarensis, walked upright but still had a small, ape-sized brain.

Eleven earlier Soviet attempts to land on the Moon had failed before Luna 9 touched down in Oceanus Procellarum on 3 February 1966. It transmitted panoramic images across seven radio sessions, showing rocks and a horizon less than a mile away, proof the surface could bear a craft's weight.

Britain got to see the pictures first. Astronomers at Jodrell Bank Observatory recognised the signal as a standard fax format, decoded it themselves, and released the images to newspapers before Soviet authorities made their own announcement, to Moscow's evident irritation.

A Peruvian explorer named Agustin Lizarraga had already scratched his name and the year 1902 into a wall at Machu Picchu, nine years before Hiram Bingham arrived. When Bingham reached the site on 24 July 1911, a local farmer, Melchor Arteaga, led him up the mountain, and two Quechua families were already farming its ancient terraces.

Bingham first credited Lizarraga's earlier visit in his own notes, then wrote him out of the story; by his 1952 book he was presenting himself as the site's finder outright. What he genuinely did was publicise it, through a National Geographic issue devoted entirely to the ruins in 1913, turning a place local farmers already worked into an international sensation.

Macrobius left almost no trace of his own life: he wrote only that he was born under a foreign sky, held the rank of vir clarissimus et inlustris, and dedicated his work to his son Eustachius. Scholars still argue over whether he came from Greek Egypt or Roman North Africa.

His Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, written around 430, used Cicero's tale as a frame for Stoic and Neoplatonic cosmology, describing the harmony of the celestial spheres and the soul's descent through the planets. Copied throughout the Middle Ages, it carried much of that Greek philosophy into Latin Europe long after the originals were lost.

Magellan never finished the voyage that carries his name. He was killed on Mactan in the Philippines in April 1521, speared and then cut down on a beach, roughly halfway through the three-year journey he had begun with five ships in September 1519.

Command passed to Juan Sebastian Elcano, who brought the last surviving ship, the Victoria, home to Spain in September 1522. Of about 270 men who set out, only 18 or 19 returned on board her, the sole ship of the original five to complete the full circuit.

Ground convex discs of glass, thick at the centre and thinner at the edge, had been used to magnify since antiquity, but it was Italian glassmakers of the thirteenth century who turned the shape into a handheld tool that monks, copyists and merchants could rely on for close work. Venice and its glassworking centre on Murano supplied much of this trade across medieval Europe.

A single lens held over a page or a ledger let an ageing scribe keep reading and a jeweller keep working fine detail long after unaided eyesight failed. The same lens shape, ground to a stronger curve and mounted in a frame worn on the face, produced the earliest eyeglasses within a few decades, so the handheld glass and the spectacle share one optical ancestor.

Flemish and south German clockmakers of the early 1400s coiled a flat strip of tempered steel that pushed back as it was wound tight with a key, storing the energy a hanging weight had always supplied. Nuremberg locksmith Peter Henlein is later credited with refining the mechanism enough to build a clock small enough to carry in the hand.

A weight-driven clock had to hang plumb and needed somewhere for the cord to fall, which ruled out ships, pockets and any wall without floor space beneath it. The spring's drawback was uneven pull as it unwound, strongest fully wound and weakest nearly spent, which clockmakers offset with a tapered pulley called a fusee so timekeeping stayed roughly steady throughout.

Maize was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in southern Mexico thousands of years earlier, and its cultivation reached far beyond that origin, north into what is now the United States and south through the Andes. Farmers bred varieties suited to different growing seasons and altitudes, adapting a single crop to highland Peru as much as to river valleys in eastern North America.

The crop's spread reshaped diets and settlement: it stores well, yields more calories per acre than many alternatives, and let denser populations settle in one place. Grown alongside beans and squash in a pairing later farmers called the three sisters, it became the calorie base for societies from Mississippian mound builders to Andean states, adapted independently by each rather than copied from one centre.

Portuguese ships carried maize from the Americas along their African and Asian trading routes during the sixteenth century, dropping it at ports where local farmers could test it against crops already suited to the soil and rainfall. Unlike wheat, maize tolerated a wide range of climates and produced more calories per acre than many established grains.

Within a few generations it had become a staple across parts of West Africa and had reached India and China, entering local cuisines so thoroughly that its American origin was often forgotten. Its productivity also let population grow in regions where earlier crops had struggled, though a heavy reliance on it in later centuries left some communities vulnerable to nutritional deficiencies when maize replaced a more varied diet.

The only source for this voyage is the Egyptian official al-Umari, who wrote that Mansa Musa, visiting Cairo on his 1324 pilgrimage, described how he had come to the throne: his predecessor had sailed a large fleet out into the Atlantic to find its far shore and never returned. No other Arab chronicle or West African oral tradition mentions the expedition, and no wreck or artefact has ever confirmed it.

The predecessor is usually named Abu Bakr II, but that ruler never existed under that title. A nineteenth-century French translator misread a genealogy in Ibn Khaldun, turning an ancestor named Abu Bakr into a king between Musa and his true predecessor, Muhammad ibn Qu. Whatever the king's real name, al-Umari's account remains the only trace of the voyage itself.

Manioc pollen turns up at San Andres in the Gulf of Mexico lowlands by around 4600 BC, and the plant itself was domesticated far earlier in west-central Brazil from a wild relative of the shrub. By the time Columbus reached the Caribbean, Taino farmers were growing it as a dependable root crop across the islands, alongside communities in northern South America and southern Mesoamerica.

The Taino processed the bitter varieties by grating and pressing out the toxic juice before baking the flour into flat cassava bread, a technique later adopted by Spanish colonists. That bread became durable enough to provision ships, and its production in Cuba is often described as the first industry the Spanish organised on the island, feeding sailors on Atlantic crossings long after 1492.

A manor's arable land split three ways: the lord's own demesne, worked for his household; peasant holdings owing labour or produce for their strips; and, on some manors, free tenants who owed only money rent. Villagers worked scattered strips in shared open fields rather than fenced plots of their own.

Villeins, the most common tenants, were unfree but not enslaved: local custom fixed what they owed and protected certain rights, a status distinct from both freeholder and slave. The system traced back to the Roman villa estate and only broke down as a cash economy spread through the later Middle Ages, replacing labour service with rent that tenants could pay from wages.

Insular script took shape in Irish monasteries during the seventh century and travelled with missionaries to Northumbria and the continent, reaching houses such as Bobbio and Wearmouth-Jarrow. Scribes there developed a distinct set of letterforms, and the tradition's flourishing stretch, roughly 600 to 850, produced the Book of Kells and the Lindisfarne Gospels.

The books were not private reading but liturgical objects, copied and decorated to honour the text they carried. Initial letters grew large and dense with interlace, dwindling in size across a page in what scholars call the diminuendo effect, a device that spread from Ireland into manuscript workshops across the continent.

Radiocarbon dates from a burial ground at Wairau Bar, on the South Island, cluster around 1288 to 1300, among the earliest firm evidence of people living in New Zealand. Pollen cores from the North Island show forest burning from around 1280, which some researchers read as the arrival itself, though the link to human activity there is not settled.

The voyagers came from tropical East Polynesia, sailing several thousand kilometres south into a temperate climate with no coconut, breadfruit or taro to rely on. Within a few generations they had adapted their crops and hunting to a cooler landscape holding giant flightless moa, which were hunted to extinction within roughly a century of settlement.

Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh spent nearly five hours sinking through the Challenger Deep inside the bathyscaphe Trieste on 23 January 1960, descending at less than a metre a second in total darkness. Around 9,000 metres down, one of the vessel's outer plexiglass windows cracked with a shudder that shook the whole craft, and the two men chose to keep descending rather than turn back.

They reached the bottom, roughly 10,900 metres by later measurement, and stayed only twenty minutes before starting the three hour climb back up. Piccard reported seeing a flatfish on the seabed, a claim later biologists have doubted since no fish is known to survive pressure that extreme; Walsh himself later conceded their identification may simply have been wrong.

John Harrison was a carpenter by trade with no formal training in horology when he began building clocks accurate enough to survive a rolling ship. His fourth attempt, H4, crossed the Atlantic in 1761 and lost only about five seconds a day, a sailor's watch rather than a cabinet clock.

Parliament had offered a reward under the Longitude Act of 1714 for a method precise enough to fix a ship's position at sea, but the board overseeing it kept demanding further trials. Harrison collected the bulk of the money only in 1773, at eighty, after King George III intervened on his behalf.

Full astronomical astrolabes carried too many engraved rings and moving parts to survive a rolling deck, so Portuguese navigators stripped the instrument down to a single heavy ring, weighted at the bottom to hang steady, with a rotating sighting bar called an alidade.

A sailor held it up by a thumb ring and sighted the sun or a known star through the alidade, then read the angle above the horizon off the scale to work out latitude. Longitude stayed unsolved for another two centuries. The earliest known surviving example, recovered from a Portuguese shipwreck off Al Hallaniyah, Oman, is dated to between 1496 and 1501.

Radiocarbon dating once put Polynesian voyagers on the Marquesas by around 300 CE, an estimate long treated as the anchor for the whole eastern Pacific migration. Newer work using only short-lived plant remains, not driftwood or old wood charcoal, points instead to the eleventh or twelfth century, roughly eight centuries later than once assumed.

Wherever the true date falls, the archipelago's isolation, over three thousand kilometres from any other inhabited shore, makes it one of the strongest test cases for how Pacific navigators found land without instruments. Genetic and linguistic evidence still ties Marquesan settlers to later voyages that reached Hawaii and Rapa Nui, so the debate over timing changes how those onward journeys are dated too.

NASA's Curiosity rover reached Gale Crater on 6 August 2012 by way of a landing sequence never used before: a rocket-powered descent stage hovered above the surface and lowered the one-tonne rover on cables, then cut them and flew off to crash a safe distance away. Engineers called the manoeuvre the sky crane, and it worked on the first attempt.

The mission was built to judge whether Gale Crater could once have supported microbial life, not to search for life directly. Within its first year the rover found evidence of an ancient freshwater lake bed on Mars, and a mission planned to last two years is still working more than a decade on.

The problem was a hot object glowing the wrong colour on paper. Existing equations for black-body radiation matched experiments at low frequencies and broke down completely at high ones, a failure physicists had no fix for using continuous energy.

In December 1900 Planck found that the numbers worked if energy could only be emitted in fixed packets, sized by frequency multiplied by a constant he called h. He treated it as a mathematical trick to fit the curve, not a claim about reality, and quantum physics grew out of an assumption its own author distrusted.

Hiram Maxim had been knocked flat by a rifle's recoil as a boy, and he later credited that jolt with the idea behind his gun: rather than fight the kick of firing, use it. Each shot's own recoil threw the breech open, ejected the spent case, loaded the next round and closed the breech again.

Patented across 1883 and 1885, the mechanism meant a single barrel could fire continuously as long as a belt of ammunition and a finger on the trigger held out, with no hand-cranking required between shots. Earlier rapid-fire weapons like the Gatling gun still needed a crank turned by hand; Maxim's ran on the energy of its own firing.

James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 paper treated electricity and magnetism as a single field rather than two separate forces, and the equations describing that field produced a wave travelling at a fixed speed. When Maxwell calculated that speed from measured electrical constants, it matched the known speed of light.

That match let him state plainly that light itself was an electromagnetic wave, propagating through the same field that carried electric and magnetic effects. The theory predicted waves at other frequencies too, which Heinrich Hertz detected experimentally more than twenty years later, confirming radio waves before anyone had a use for them.

Maya astronomers tracked the moon's cycle to about 29.5302 days, against a true value of 29.5306, a figure precise enough that their lunar calendar held up over long stretches without correction. The Dresden Codex, a bark-paper book that survived the Spanish burning of Maya texts, records tables built around the 819-day count, used to align the cycles of the visible planets against each other.

Its Venus table tracks that planet's synodic period, roughly 584 days, closely enough to anticipate its reappearance as morning or evening star over generations, information tied to the timing of rituals and warfare in Maya cities. The refinements credited to the eighth century built on centuries of recorded observation rather than a single breakthrough, correcting small drifts that had accumulated in the Long Count system.

A Long Count date carved at Chiapa de Corzo, in Mexico, from 36 BCE already needs a marker for an empty position, though no Maya inscription is known to use a zero glyph, a shell shape, before the third century CE. Some scholars credit the surrounding Olmec culture with the earlier invention, since the eight oldest Long Count dates all come from outside the Maya heartland.

Maya scribes used the shell zero within a base-twenty, place-value system to track dates across tens of thousands of years. It was one of at least three independent inventions of positional zero worldwide, alongside Babylon and India, and reached Europe centuries later only through Arabic mathematics, not through any contact with the Americas.

Maya priest-astronomers timed Venus's appearances as morning and evening star closely enough that their calendar corrections kept the count accurate over centuries, a table preserved in the Dresden Codex, one of only four Maya books to survive the Spanish burnings of the sixteenth century. Their estimate of the synodic month was closer to the modern value than the figure Ptolemy used in Alexandria centuries earlier.

The Dresden Codex also contains tables predicting eclipses and tracking Venus's 584-day cycle against the 260-day ritual calendar, a coordination that let priests time wars and sacrifices to the planet's appearance as morning star. None of this rested on instruments; observers used naked-eye sightings of the horizon recorded over generations.

Maya astronomers tracked the 584-day cycle of Venus closely enough that the Dresden Codex records its risings and settings across a table spanning roughly 104 years, correcting for drift as the count ran on. Separate tables in the same codex predicted eclipses over a span of about thirty-three years and tracked a 780-day Mars cycle.

Observations were made from purpose-built structures such as the Caracol at Chichen Itza, whose windows align with the extreme positions of Venus on the horizon, and from buildings oriented to solstice and equinox sunrises elsewhere. Their calendar's estimate of the solar year was close enough that it outperformed the calendar the Spanish brought with them on contact.

The Mayflower carried about 102 passengers and thirty crew when it dropped anchor off Cape Cod on 21 November 1620, weeks after leaving England and far north of the Virginia land grant it was aiming for. Only around half the passengers were the separatist congregation later called Pilgrims; the rest were hired hands, servants and families travelling for ordinary reasons.

Before anyone went ashore, 41 of the men signed the Mayflower Compact, a short agreement to form a civil body and obey its future laws, written because the ship had landed outside the territory its royal charter covered. The first winter killed roughly half the settlers, and the survivors' colony at Plymouth outlived them by generations.

Egyptian builders worked to the royal cubit, a rod roughly 52.4 centimetres long and marked off into seven palms of four fingers each. Surviving examples vary by only a few millimetres across centuries of use, evidence of rods being checked against a master standard rather than copied freely by hand.

One such rod belonged to Maya, treasurer to Tutankhamun, and was buried with him at Saqqara; another turned up in the tomb of the architect Kha at Thebes. Builders used these rods to lay out structures as early as Djoser's Step Pyramid, keeping walls and chambers consistent across a project that took years to complete.

Blaise Pascal built the machine at eighteen to ease his father's work as a tax official in Rouen, linking a row of dials with gears so that carrying a ten from one column into the next happened automatically as a wheel completed a turn.

Pascal produced roughly twenty of the machines over the following decade, of which nine survive today. The Pascaline could add and subtract directly; multiplication and division required repeated addition, a limitation later calculators, including Leibniz's stepped-drum machine, tried to overcome.

No first clock survives. The earliest picture of a weight-driven one is an illustration in the Bible of St Louis, made between 1226 and 1234, showing the fall of the weight slowed by water turning a wheel. No working example from that period survives.

By 1271 the English astronomer Robertus Anglicus wrote that craftsmen were trying to build a wheel that would turn once a day using gravity alone, without yet managing it reliably. The idea combined gearing and striking mechanisms already known from European and Islamic astronomical instruments.

Cyrus McCormick gave the first public demonstration of his reaper in 1831 at Steeles Tavern, Virginia, but it took until 1834 to secure a patent, and even then nobody bought one. Early versions jammed and stalled on uneven ground, and years of quiet redesign passed before the machine could be trusted on a real harvest.

Sales only picked up in the 1840s, once the design had been reworked for varied terrain and crops. By 1856 McCormick's factory was turning out more than four thousand reapers a year, mostly bound for the flat, expanding wheat farms of the American Midwest, and the machine cut the number of hands a farm needed to bring in a harvest.

Lewis Paul held the 1738 patent alone; John Wyatt built the machine to Paul's idea rather than co-owning the rights. Rollers turning at different speeds drew cotton fibre out to a controlled thickness before a spindle twisted it, replacing the human hand's stretch-and-twist with a mechanical one for the first time.

The idea worked better than the business behind it. Paul licensed mills, including Edward Cave's at Northampton, but profits stayed thin and most had closed or changed use by the 1760s. Roller spinning itself survived: Richard Arkwright built his far more successful water frame around the same rollers three decades later.

Melanesia's islands, from New Guinea through the Solomons to Vanuatu and Fiji, had been settled for tens of thousands of years while Polynesian voyagers were still reaching the remote Pacific, giving the region far greater linguistic and genetic diversity than islands settled later. Its communities were not isolated: obsidian, shell ornaments and pottery moved along established sea routes between islands hundreds of kilometres apart.

The Lapita culture, whose pottery marks the archaeological trail through the region several thousand years earlier, had given way to more localised island societies with their own trading languages and exchange systems. What survives of this trade is mostly archaeological, since Melanesian societies left no written record and European accounts only begin centuries later.

Gregor Mendel's 1866 paper on pea plants laid out ratios of inherited traits that would become the foundation of genetics, and almost nobody noticed. It was cited perhaps three times in the following thirty five years, filed away in a provincial natural history journal most biologists never opened.

Three separate researchers, working independently, arrived at similar conclusions and rediscovered Mendel's paper within two months of each other in 1900, decades after his death. Only then did his counting of wrinkled and smooth peas become the starting point of a science, rather than a monk's overlooked hobby.

Alcohol thermometers of the early 1700s drifted and disagreed with each other, since no two instrument makers used the same fixed points. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who had been building spirit thermometers since around 1706, began working with mercury around 1713 and found it expanded more evenly with heat.

He anchored his scale with three points: a salt and ice mixture at zero, the temperature at which still water starts to freeze at thirty two, and roughly the temperature of the human body near the top. By 1721 his manufacturing was consistent enough that two of his thermometers, made years apart, would finally agree.

Mysore's rockets replaced the bamboo tube of earlier gunpowder rockets with an iron cylinder, letting Hyder Ali's forces pack in more propellant and fire it under higher pressure. At the Battle of Pollilur in 1780 the rockets skimmed along the ground into East India Company ranks, breaking formations that muskets and cannon had not managed to break first.

When Mysore's capital fell in 1799, British forces captured thousands of rockets and launchers and shipped examples home for study. William Congreve used them to design his own iron rockets for the Royal Artillery in 1805, the weapons Britain later fired at Baltimore in 1814, the attack remembered in the American national anthem.

In the early 1870s the French engineer Gustave Trouve adapted an induction-balance circuit, already used to hunt for bullets lodged in wounded soldiers, into a handheld device whose buzzer changed tone over lead as against iron. It was among the first instruments built specifically to sense buried or hidden metal rather than just electrify a bell.

The same principle was tried, unsuccessfully, on a president: in 1881 Alexander Graham Bell built a similar induction-balance coil to find the bullet lodged in James Garfield after his shooting, but the metal bed frame Garfield lay on confused the reading. Bell's coil design nonetheless became the ancestor of later handheld detectors.

A law of 7 April 1795 fixed the metre as one ten millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along a meridian through Paris, and the gramme as the weight of one cubic centimetre of water. Surveyors spent years remeasuring that meridian to fix the standard, and platinum bars embodying the metre and kilogram were not deposited in the national archives until 1799.

Adoption was not instant or popular. Traders kept using old regional units informally, and in 1812 Napoleon allowed a hybrid system with familiar names attached to metric values before the decimal system was made compulsory again later. The metric system did not become France's sole legal standard in practice until well into the nineteenth century.

Johann Maelzel patented his metronome in 1815, a year after a Dutch inventor, Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel, built a spring-driven inverted pendulum in Amsterdam that kept the same kind of steady beat. Maelzel added a numbered scale to Winkel's mechanism and began manufacturing the pyramid-shaped device under his own name in 1816.

Winkel never patented his version, and Maelzel's branding stuck so completely that the device is still called Maelzel's Metronome in old scores, marked simply MM. Composers from Beethoven onward used the numbered scale to fix a tempo precisely, replacing vague Italian terms like allegro with a beat count a performer could set on the device itself.

Near the equator, navigators saw the whole sky wheel overhead through a night, which let them memorise a chain of rising and setting stars for each route and hold a course by watching which one sat on the horizon ahead. Ocean swells, steadier than wind-driven waves, gave a second reference that worked even under cloud.

In the Marshall Islands this knowledge took physical form as stick charts: coconut-frond midribs lashed into a frame, with shells marking islands and the sticks showing how swells bent and crossed around them. Each chart was largely legible only to the navigator who built it, and the practice died out after the Second World War as instruments took over.

Navigators across the Caroline Islands memorised the point on the horizon where particular stars rose and set, building a mental star compass that let them hold a course through open water without instruments. Swells, more consistent than local wind-driven waves, gave a second, tactile way to check direction after clouds hid the sky.

On Marshall Islands, navigators built stick charts from lashed coconut fronds and cowrie shells to show how islands bent incoming swells, though a chart's meaning belonged to whoever made it rather than to any shared code. The knowledge passed orally between master and apprentice; Mau Piailug later taught it to a new generation of Pacific navigators from the 1970s onward.

The chip that made personal computers possible was commissioned to run a desktop calculator. Japan's Busicom asked Intel for a set of custom chips for a printing calculator, and engineer Marcian Hoff proposed replacing that whole set with one general-purpose processor instead, a design Federico Faggin then turned into working silicon.

Intel released the result, the 4004, on 15 November 1971. It packed 2,300 transistors and ran at roughly 740 kilohertz, feeble even by the standards of a few years later, but it proved that a computer's entire central processing unit could fit on a single chip rather than filling a cabinet.

No single name survives with certainty for the first compound microscope. The claim usually attaches to the Dutch spectacle-makers Hans and Zacharias Janssen around 1590, but the account comes chiefly from Zacharias's son decades later, and rival spectacle makers in the same Dutch towns have their own supporters among historians.

What is firmer is the technique: mounting two lenses in a tube so the image from one is magnified by the other, a trick spectacle workshops were well placed to stumble on. Within decades the idea had spread across Europe, and by the 1670s it let Antonie van Leeuwenhoek grind single lenses powerful enough to see bacteria for the first time.

Percy Spencer had no formal schooling past grammar level; he was orphaned young and taught himself physics and electrical engineering while serving in the navy. At Raytheon he worked on magnetrons, the tubes that generate radar's microwaves, and later recalled that a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he stood near an active set, though no contemporary record confirms the story.

Whatever prompted it, Spencer tested the effect deliberately, popping corn and exploding an egg with microwave energy, then built a metal box to contain the field. Raytheon filed a patent in October 1945 and sold the first commercial model, the Radarange, in 1947. It stood six feet tall, weighed 750 pounds and cost about 5,000 dollars.

Lion Cavern at Ngwenya, in what is now Eswatini, is generally cited as the world's oldest known mine. Radiocarbon dating of material from the site put the earliest extraction of specular haematite at roughly 41,000 to 43,000 years ago, with some artefacts from earlier excavations estimated at over 20,000 years old.

The ore was not smelted for metal; it was crushed for red ochre pigment, valued for its colour and reflective shine, and used in cosmetics and ritual by Middle Stone Age communities. Much later, San rock painters in the same region drew on ochre from the same deposits, a continuity of use spanning tens of thousands of years at one hillside.

On 11 July 1405, Zheng He led the first of what would become seven expeditions out of China, commanding fleets of hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men, dwarfing anything Portugal or Spain would send to sea for another century. The voyages reached Southeast Asia, India, the Arabian Peninsula and the coast of East Africa, collecting tribute and exotic goods for the Yongle Emperor's court.

Each fleet mixed diplomacy with a clear show of force, installing friendly rulers in some ports and putting down opposition in others, all while charting sea routes that Chinese merchants had sailed for generations. Zheng He himself, a Muslim eunuch from Yunnan raised in the imperial household, commanded every voyage, tying the whole enterprise to his own standing at court as much as to any lasting Ming policy.

Mir's core module reached orbit on 20 February 1986, the first space station built to grow by docking extra modules onto it over time rather than launching complete in one piece. Designed for roughly five years of service, it kept flying for fifteen, deorbited only in March 2001.

Across its life Mir hosted 105 cosmonauts and astronauts from twelve countries and logged eighty spacewalks. Cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov spent 437 consecutive days aboard between 1994 and 1995, still the longest single human spaceflight, while the Shuttle-Mir programme later put American crews on the station during the final years of Cold War-era space rivalry.

Nokia's 9000 Communicator went on sale in August 1996, a clamshell phone that opened to reveal a full keyboard and screen wide enough for a web page. Its modem pulled data over the GSM network at 9.6 kilobits a second, slower than most home dial-up connections of the day.

Its browser could not render most sites properly, since the web of 1996 was built for desktop monitors rather than a phone's small monochrome screen, so pages arrived as dense text with images stripped out. The device sold mainly to business travellers rather than the wider public.

The Moche engineered canals that crossed entire valley systems on Peru's north coast, one of the driest strips of land on Earth, carrying meltwater and groundwater from Andean rivers out onto desert terraces. The Ascope aqueduct and La Cumbre canal in the Chicama valley are among the surviving works, some still watering fields today.

Keeping the system running took coordinated labour across whole valleys, work that likely fell to communities under local lords rather than a single central state. Tree-ring and ice-core evidence points to a prolonged drought around the sixth century, followed by heavy El Nino flooding, and both have been linked to the disruption of southern Moche centres.

Archaeological finds from Roman Britain show a heavy, wheeled plough with an iron share by the third or fourth century, well before its wider use further north. It cut deep furrows in the wet, dense clay soils of northern Europe that lighter Mediterranean ploughs could barely scratch, turning the sod itself rather than merely scoring it.

Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than most single households owned, so neighbours pooled teams and land was reorganised into long open strips worked in common. Wider adoption tracked the spread of three-field rotation in the late eighth and early ninth centuries, and the cooperation it forced helped shape the manorial villages of medieval Europe.

Northern Europe's heavy clay soils defeated the old scratch plough, which merely scored the surface rather than turning it. A heavy iron mouldboard design, first recorded in Han China, spread westward and by the later Middle Ages was mounted on wheels, letting the plough carry more weight and drag a larger, metal-faced mouldboard through ground that would have stalled a lighter frame.

Pulling one of these ploughs took a team of four to eight oxen, reshaping how villages organised labour and land: strips were ploughed communally because no single household kept a full team. The wooden mouldboard itself stayed largely unchanged until Joseph Foljambe's iron-faced Rotherham plough arrived in the eighteenth century, three hundred years after the medieval improvements described here.

Cassiodorus, a Roman statesman turned monk, built his monastery at Vivarium in the sixth century with sundials, water clocks and lamps kept burning through the night so his monks could keep copying texts. Not every monastery had a dedicated scriptorium, a writing room; scribes often worked instead in a library or their own cells, copying the Vulgate and the works of the Church Fathers by hand.

The labour was divided: some monks prepared parchment, others copied the text line by line, others added illumination. A tenth-century prior described the toll bluntly: it dimmed the eyes, ached the back and knitted the chest and belly together. Monte Cassino later grew into the largest centre of book production in southern Italy, and such houses are why many classical texts survived Rome's collapse at all.

Arab and Persian sailors crossing the Indian Ocean depended on monsoon winds that reverse direction with the seasons, blowing toward Asia through the summer and back toward Africa and Arabia in winter. Their lateen-rigged dhows, triangular-sailed ships already in use for centuries, could sail closer to the wind than square-rigged vessels and were built around this seasonal reversal rather than fighting it.

A round trip meant timing departure to ride one monsoon out and the other back, sometimes waiting months in a foreign port for the wind to turn. Sailors judged position using the kamal, a simple wooden card on a string that measured a star's height above the horizon, alongside dead reckoning, well before the compass and astrolabe became common tools on these same routes.

Knowledge that Indian Ocean winds reverse with the seasons, blowing from the southwest in summer and the northeast in winter, was already old by the eighth century, but Abbasid-era sailors used it to run scheduled voyages rather than opportunistic ones. Siraf, on the Persian Gulf coast of Iran, was the trade's main terminal: ships left on the outbound monsoon and waited months at the far end for the wind to turn before sailing home.

That timing made a single round trip from the Gulf to southern China, the route described in the ninth-century compilation Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind, take the better part of two years. Cargo moved the other way too: Chinese ceramics recovered from a wreck off Belitung in Indonesia, dated to around 830, show the scale of goods a single Arab-built ship could carry.

Armstrong stepped off the ladder at 20:17:40 UTC on 20 July 1969, roughly six hours after the Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility. His line, that's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind, went out live to an estimated 25 million viewers in the United States alone.

Buzz Aldrin joined him nineteen minutes later, and together they spent two and a half hours outside the module, collecting rock samples and planting a flag stiffened with wire because there was no air to make it hang. Michael Collins circled overhead alone in the command module, never setting foot on the surface.

Friedrich Serturner was a young pharmacist's assistant in Paderborn when he isolated a crystalline compound from opium resin around 1804, first testing it on a mouse and three dogs, one of which died. Years later he dosed himself and three boys, none older than seventeen, and all of them fell dangerously ill. He named the substance morphium after Morpheus, the god of dreams.

Chemists before Serturner had treated plant extracts as mixtures too complex to purify. His isolation showed that a single active compound inside a crude drug could be extracted, weighed and dosed precisely, a method chemists then applied to strychnine, quinine and caffeine within the following two decades.
